Plus, Nvidia in turmoil, and DoorDash competes with Amazon
 

Good morning, I’m filling in for Spencer Jakab. Markets are grappling with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s confirmation of an affair and the board’s investigation into reports he was an espionage target. Nvidia’s shares are down premarket; if they don’t recover, the company’s year-to-date gains could evaporate. Despite this, Nasdaq futures are fighting to stay positive, and Dow and S&P futures are in the green. One tailwind, oil is down again.

Buckle up

 

The fine print on Boeing’s big acquisition last year keeps getting uglier.

 

In late October, the jet maker reported a $123 million pretax loss for the third quarter, and its stock got trounced. Management dialed back expectations for free cash flow and plane deliveries, and Boeing’s core commercial-airplanes unit posted a $697 million operating loss.

 

But, once again, not all of Boeing’s red ink showed up on the income statement, and the costliest surprises trace back to its purchase of Spirit AeroSystems, its longtime fuselage supplier.

 

Boeing’s stumbles show how difficult turnarounds can be for investors to time. Its shares are down 60% since peaking in 2019.

 

The Spirit deal was supposed to be part of Boeing’s comeback story. It owned Spirit’s factories once before, selling the operations in 2005 to pursue an outsourcing and cost-cutting strategy that ultimately backfired. Buying Spirit was meant to bring more of its manufacturing in-house.

 

During the first half of 2026, Boeing had already uncovered hundreds of millions of dollars in liabilities at Spirit beyond what it initially recognized when the deal closed in December. Last quarter, it found even more.

 

The higher obligations represent real losses, because they mean greater costs for Boeing on deeply unfavorable contracts at below-market prices. 

 

To date, Boeing has kept the growing costs related to Spirit off its income statement through a quirk in accounting rules. It won’t have that option much longer.

 

Once a company completes an acquisition, it gets 12 months to adjust its purchase-price allocation without booking an immediate expense. After that one-year window closes, any newly discovered losses must be recognized in full.

 

Boeing closed its purchase of Spirit on Dec. 8, 2025. It paid $8.4 billion and initially determined the acquired assets’ fair value was $1.6 billion less than the combined liabilities. So the company recorded $10 billion of goodwill, representing the difference between the purchase price and Spirit’s net identifiable assets, which were negative.

 

By midyear, the deficit had grown. As of June 30, Boeing said the identifiable assets’ fair value was $1.9 billion less than the combined liabilities; it lifted the goodwill to $10.3 billion.

 

Boeing made further adjustments last quarter, raising the deficit to $2.2 billion and goodwill to $10.6 billion as of Sept. 30, exceeding the company’s total equity. The primary reason was a $370 million increase in the estimated liability for certain “off-market customer contracts.” Boeing offered little detail about the contracts or why they’ve become such a sinkhole.

 

After Dec. 8, any more unpleasant surprises will hit Boeing’s bottom line directly, pushing the turnaround narrative further out of reach.

One Big Chart

 
 
 
 

DoorDash is suddenly competing with Amazon on multiple fronts. Late last month, DoorDash announced a deal to buy Instacart for $17 billion, valuing the grocery delivery platform at a 26% premium to pre-deal rumor prices. The combined company would have a 19% market share in U.S. online grocery sales, according to data from Emarketer.

 

DoorDash’s shares had dipped following news of a rumored deal, but rallied in the days following the deal announcement. Then on Thursday, news of an Amazon-Uber Eats partnership sent DoorDash shares plunging 9.4%. The selloff appears overdone.
